steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a machine learning paper on neural k-forms: learning representations of simplicial complexes embedded in R^n by integrating learnable differential forms instead of message passing. Cover the limits of message passing in geometric deep learning, our key idea, a paper outline, and related work on higher-order GNNs.

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Geometric deep learning has extended deep learning methods so that they include information about the geometry of data, and to a lesser extent the topology, which made it possible to use them in more complicated and richer domains like graphs. In recent years a plethora of methods have been developed, but message passing is still the predominant paradigm of the field, and it was recently extended to higher-order domains, including simplicial complexes, cell complexes, and hypergraphs. But even though it is useful, the message passing paradigm has inherent limitations like over-smoothing, over-squashing, and not being able to capture long-range dependencies. Because of these limitations we often need strategies like graph rewiring, which change the underlying graph structure and so affect generalisation performance.

Our paper goes a completely different way and tries to use additional geometric information from a data set to get robust and interpretable representations of the input data. Specifically, the input data we consider are simplicial complexes embedded in \mathbb{R}^{n} via node coordinates. This kind of complex can be built from any graph with node features, for example, where the node features act as the coordinates. Our key insight is to use differential k -forms in \mathbb{R}^{n}. A k -form in \mathbb{R}^{n} can be integrated over any k -simplex embedded in \mathbb{R}^{n}, and this gives a real number. So an \ell -tuple of k -forms gives an \ell -dimensional representation of the simplex, and this does not depend on any message passing. Seen this way, k -forms are globally consistent feature maps over the space of embedded k -simplices, and they have the geometric semantics and interpretability of integration. This lets us use tools from differential geometry to prove a version of universal approximation and a number of other theoretical results. Also, the structure of differential forms in \mathbb{R}^{n} makes learning algorithms (computationally) feasible. In particular, a multi-layer perceptron with the right dimensions induces a k -form on \mathbb{R}^{n} which can be integrated. This means that learnable, finitely-parametrised differential forms can be put into existing machine learning libraries and applied to common tasks in geometric deep learning. We find that our method is better at using information from geometrical graphs than existing message passing neural networks. Our method is efficient, and it is also generally applicable to many kinds of input complexes, including graphs, simplicial complexes, and cell complexes.

- Outline
  - Section 2 background: simplicial complexes, differential forms
  - Section 3 neural k -forms, universal approximation; integration matrix; propositions from properties of integration
  - Section 4 basic architecture, algorithms
  - Section 5 intuitive experiments + benchmarks on standard geometrical DL data sets
- Related work
  - generalising GNNs to higher dimensions: simplicial neural networks (cite); methods using higher-order topological features (cite); optimisation algorithms for representations of simplicial complexes (cite)
  - all use diffusion processes or message passing on simplicial complexes
  - extensions to cell complexes (cite), cellular sheaves (cite)
  - limitations from message passing / aggregation along combinatorial structure
  - over-smoothing (regression to the mean for node features, indistinguishable), over-squashing (can't transport long-range node info) -> extra interventions (cite)

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:

Section 2 gives the relevant background on simplicial complexes and differential forms. Section 3 introduces neural k -forms and proves a universal approximation statement. We also show there how neural k -forms induce a so-called integration matrix, and we use the properties of integration to prove some propositions. Section 4 presents the basic architecture and algorithms. Finally, Section 5 has several intuitive experiments and benchmarks of our method on standard geometrical deep learning data sets.

There are several methods that generalise graph neural networks (GNNs) to higher-dimensional domains. These include simplicial neural networks, methods that can use higher-order topological features of data, and optimisation algorithms for learning representations of simplicial complexes. All these methods work on simplicial complexes through diffusion processes or message passing algorithms. Some works also extend message passing or aggregation schemes to cell complexes or to cellular sheaves. But these existing methods have limitations that come from using message passing or aggregation along a combinatorial structure. Message passing often leads to over-smoothing (all node features regress to the mean and become indistinguishable) or over-squashing (long-range node information can't be transported through the graph), and this needs additional interventions. So there is a need for methods that go beyond message passing. Our work gives a novel perspective based on integrating learnable k -forms on combinatorial domains like graphs or simplicial complexes embedded in \mathbb{R}^{n}, i.e. we assume that (vertex) coordinates exist.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Geometric deep learning [1] expanded the scope of deep learning methods to include information about the geometry, and to a lesser extent the topology, of data, thus enabling their use in more complicated and richer domains like graphs. While recent years have seen the development of a plethora of methods, the predominant paradigm of the field remains message passing [2], which was recently extended to handle higher-order domains, including simplicial complexes [3], cell complexes [4], and hypergraphs [5]. Despite its utility, however, the message passing paradigm suffers from inherent limitations like over-smoothing, over-squashing, and an inability to capture long-range dependencies. These limitations often require strategies like graph rewiring, which change the underlying graph structure [6,7] and thus affect generalisation performance.

Our paper pursues a completely different path, striving to leverage additional geometric information from a data set to obtain robust and interpretable representations of the input data. Specifically, we consider input data in the form of simplicial complexes embedded in \mathbb{R}^{n} via node coordinates. Such a complex can be built from any graph with node features, for example, with the node features acting as the coordinates. Our key insight is the use of differential k -forms in \mathbb{R}^{n}. A k -form in \mathbb{R}^{n} can be integrated over any k -simplex embedded in \mathbb{R}^{n} to produce a real number. Thus an \ell -tuple of k -forms produces an \ell -dimensional representation of the simplex independently of any message passing. From this perspective, k -forms play the role of globally consistent feature maps over the space of embedded k -simplices, possessing the geometric semantics and interpretability of integration. This enables us to use tools from differential geometry to prove a version of universal approximation, along with a number of other theoretical results. Moreover, the structure of differential forms in \mathbb{R}^{n} makes learning algorithms (computationally) feasible: a multi-layer perceptron with the right dimensions induces a k -form on \mathbb{R}^{n} that can be integrated. This implies that learnable, finitely-parametrised differential forms can be integrated into existing machine learning libraries and applied to common tasks in geometric deep learning. We find that our method is better at harnessing information from geometrical graphs than existing message passing neural networks. Besides being efficient, our method is also generally applicable to a wide variety of input complexes, including graphs, simplicial complexes, and cell complexes.

We present the relevant background on simplicial complexes and differential forms in Section 2. In Section 3, we introduce neural k -forms and prove a universal approximation statement; we also show how neural k -forms induce a so-called integration matrix, and use the properties of integration to prove a number of propositions. Section 4 presents the basic architecture and algorithms. Finally, in Section 5, we perform several intuitive experiments and benchmark our method on standard geometrical deep learning data sets.

Several methods focus on generalising graph neural networks (GNNs) to higher-dimensional domains, proposing simplicial neural networks [3,8,9,10,11,12,13], methods that can leverage higher-order topological features of data [14,15,16], or optimisation algorithms for learning representations of simplicial complexes [17]. All of these methods operate on simplicial complexes via diffusion processes or message passing algorithms. Some works also extend message passing or aggregation schemes to cell complexes [18,4,14] or cellular sheaves [19,20]. However, these existing methods exhibit limitations that arise from the use of message passing or aggregation along a combinatorial structure. Message passing often results in over-smoothing (a regression to the mean for all node features, making them indistinguishable) or over-squashing (an inability to transport long-range node information throughout the graph), which necessitates additional interventions [6,21,7]. Hence, there is a need for methods that go beyond message passing. Our work provides a novel perspective based on the integration of learnable k -forms on combinatorial domains like graphs or simplicial complexes embedded in \mathbb{R}^{n}, i.e. we assume the existence of (vertex) coordinates.
